intervals.label: ANITA-LITE
intervals.note: End date derived by adding the stated ~18.5-day flight duration to the launch date (17 Dec 2003 + 18 d = 4 Jan 2004); not stated as a calendar date by the source.
intervals.quote: ANITA-LITE Launch Date: December 17, 2003 A prototype to the full ANITA experiment, ANITA-LITE, was flown for ~18.5 days onboard a NASA LDB scientific balooon during the 2003 Austral Summer from McMurdo Base, Antarctica.

intervals.label: ANITA-I
intervals.note: End date derived by adding the stated ~35-day flight duration to the launch date (15 Dec 2006 + 35 d = 19 Jan 2007); not stated as a calendar date by the source.
intervals.quote: ANITA I Launch Date: December 15, 2006 The first ANITA experiment was flown for ~35 days onboard a NASA LDB scientific balooon during the 2006-2007 Austral Summer from McMurdo Base, Antarctica.

intervals.label: ANITA-II
intervals.note: End date derived by adding the stated 31 days aloft to the launch date (21 Dec 2008 + 31 d = 21 Jan 2009); not stated as a calendar date by the source.
intervals.quote: The second ﬂight of ANITA (ANITA-II) launched from Williams Field, Antarctica on December 21, 2008 and landed near Siple Dome after 31 days aloft, resulting in 28.5 live days.

intervals.label: ANITA-III
intervals.note: Only month precision for the launch date is stated in the companion journal article; no exact end date is given, only the 22-day flight duration.
intervals.quote: The third flight of ANITA (ANITA-III) was launched in December 2014 and completed a 22-day flight.

name: ANITA payload
notes: Placement caveat repeated here from experiment:anita: the launch site is not the detection location.

placements.note: This placement records the balloon LAUNCH site only, not a detection location. ANITA is a balloon payload: it takes its actual data at float altitude (~37 km) drifting over the Antarctic continent during each multi-week flight, not at any fixed ground position. The site is recorded as the sourced launch facility with this caveat rather than left unplaced, since a real, sourced launch location exists.
placements.quote: ANITA-LITE Launch Date: December 17, 2003 A prototype to the full ANITA experiment, ANITA-LITE, was flown for ~18.5 days onboard a NASA LDB scientific balooon during the 2003 Austral Summer from McMurdo Base, Antarctica.

area.quote: Flying at 120,000ft (~ 37 km) the instrument can observe ~1.5 million square kilometers of ice while searching for radio signals originating from the Antarctic ice.

float_altitude.note: Not the Appendix A 'altitude' spec key (reserved for a fixed site/facility elevation, plausibility range -500-6000 m): this is the balloon's float altitude during flight, renamed to avoid that mismatch.

summary.plain: A ring of radio antennas hanging beneath a giant NASA balloon, floating 37 kilometres over Antarctica and listening for the radio crackle of a neutrino hitting the ice far below.
summary.technical: Balloon-borne quad-ridged horn antenna array for Askaryan-effect radio detection of UHE neutrinos and cosmic rays, flown at ~37 km altitude over Antarctica across five flights (2003-2016), launched from the NASA LDB facility near McMurdo Station.

technology.note: Quote is from the ANITA-IV paper (quad-ridge horns, Askaryan emission). The cosmic-ray-shower part of the description rests on the official instrument page, which features the publication 'Observation of Ultra-high-energy Cosmic Rays with the ANITA Balloon-borne Radio Interferometer'.
technology.quote: ANITA is sensitive to impulsive broadband radio emission from interactions of ultra-high-energy neutrinos in polar ice (Askaryan emission) ... Forty-eight dual-polarized quad-ridge horn antennas from Antenna Research Associates, Inc. are arranged in three rings
technology.value: Balloon-borne array of quad-ridged horn antennas detecting radio-frequency Askaryan-effect pulses from neutrino- and cosmic-ray-induced showers in Antarctic ice
